header.name: Reading Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit
header.description:
This course will undertake a reading of major sections of one of the foundational texts of the phenomenological tradition within Continental philosophy —the Phenomenology of Spirit, by G.W. F. Hegel. Our concern would be to understand the senses in which the text develops, and/or fails to develop Kant’s transcendental idealist turn. Hegel claims that the movement from Kant, through Fichte and Schelling, to himself, represents a necessary development that ‘completes’ Kant’s transcendental turn, and therefore, sets up a coherent, universal, reflective, and thus, non-sceptical idealism. While this Hegelian (self) interpretation is widely accepted, it is open to contention. It is against the background of this debate that we will discuss three organizing claims that Hegel presents in the text.
i) self- consciousness is necessarily mediated through the consciousness of the other, that is, self-consciousness requires intersubjectivity
ii) self-consciousness, and therefore, reflective philosophy, is nothing but the historicity of its own emergence.
iii) the basic motivation that drives experience and reflection is not epistemic or theoretical, but rather, ethical or practical.
Further, in tracing the systematic emergence of various ‘forms of consciousness’ including ‘self-consciousness’ and its dialectically ‘one-sided’ formations, culminating in its reconciliation in ‘absolute knowing’, we find that the text operates on several interconnected planes. For example, it presents a systematic, unified history of the theoretical/practical dimensions of thought/experience (thought as experience); thus, it functions as a ‘Bildungsroman’, chronicling the self-education of the spirit, and as a propaedeutic to Hegel’s own full-fledged system. One of the tertiary objectives of the course would be to disentangle these discursive themes and articulate some of the inner tensions that come to constitute distinct lines of emphasis and interpretation.
We start by examining naïve consciousness, immersed in the immediate certainty of ‘sensory’ cognition, and follow the movement and phases of its epistemic complication. We then turn to Hegel’s famous analysis (supplemented with secondary texts), of desire, work and (mis)recognition in the master-slave dialectic, to argue that it is misrecognition, as an ethical category that proves to be the driving force of the historical becoming of the worldly shapes of self-consciousness. Here, we consider the objections raised by Bataille and Derrida in relation to Hegel’s account. We follow the contours of these shapes that self-consciousness takes in ‘Reason’ and its ascent through the forms of ‘outer’ and ‘inner’ nature to Spirit (and Religion). Finally, we discuss the sense in which ‘absolute knowing’ represents a reconciliation of dialectical ‘one-sidedness’, by taking into account Kojève’s (and Fukuyama’s, following Kojève) famous ‘end of history’ thesis.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: The course will enable students to situate the text in relation to the history of western philosophy

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: The course aims to explain and make the structure of the argument/text comprehensible to students.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: The course will enable students to compare and analyse the various critiques of the Hegelian dialectic.

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: The course will enable students to critically analyse and evaluate Hegel's systematic approach, in light of 'contemporary deconstructive' tendencies against systemticity.

lecture_topics: The theme of finitude in the idea of the 'limits of possible experience'
The critique of 'limits' through the critique of the 'phenomenal-noumenal' distinction
Self-Consciousness': The self-deceptive forms of freedom: Stoicism, Scepticism, Unhappy consciousness
Spirit That is Certain of Itself: Morality'
